newsitem.title: USA: DJIA products likely to attract retail business.
newsitem.headline: DJIA products likely to attract retail business.

text.p: The three U.S. exchanges that received licenses to trade products on the Dow Jones Industrial Average will likely attract individual, rather than institutional, business, futures industry analysts said.

"It has an immediate kind of curb appeal for a retail investor because that's what they would know most about, the Dow," said Jim Collins, senior vice president for institutional financial futures at Smith Barney.

Dow Jones & Co Inc said Thursday it gave the American Stock Exchange (AMEX), the Chicago Board of Trade (CBOT) and the Chicago Board Options Exchange (CBOE) licenses to trade futures, futures on options and cash options on DJIA.
A CBOT spokesman said the exchange has already designated prime pit space in its new financial trading room.
"We plan to launch before the end of the year," he said.

Fred Grede, a CBOT senior vice president, said the exchange would apply immediately for U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission and Commodity Futures Trading Commission approval to trade DJIA futures and options on futures.

Futures analysts said retail investors will be the primary users of the listed Dow products because the Dow Jones is too narrow of an index for hedge funds and institutional money managers. "It only takes one or two stocks in the Dow to make it move quite a bit," Barrett Lewald, senior financial futures strategist at Lind-Waldock Inc, said. "I think it will probably have a better retail return."

They said the Standard & Poor's 500 index, which currently trades futures at the CBOT's cross-town rival, the Chicago Mercantile Exchange (CME), will most likely remain the benchmark for institutional and hedge fund managers.
"Obviously, we think there is a lot of appetite for institutional investors as well as (retail)," Grede said.
The price on the CBOT's IDEM seat, or Index Debt and Energy Market membership, rose to $128,000 on June 5 from $65,000 on June 4. IDEM members will be able to trade DJIA futures.

Within minutes of Dow's announcement, the CME said it was offering a mini-S&P contract. Some analysts said the contract size had grown almost eight-fold since its introduction, making it unmanageable for retail investors to trade.
One portfolio manager said any listed Dow Jones products would have a difficult time attracting institutional business.
"I don't think it will be successful because it's not capitalization weighted," he said. "The S&P is. When people have to use benchmarks, they use the S&P 500, the Wilshire 5000, the Russell 3000."
Many floor traders and industry analysts pointed to the low volume in the Major Market Index (MMI) futures contracts as an indication of the fate of DJIA products.
MMI consists of roughly 20 Dow stocks and has a 97-percent price correlation with the DJIA.
The CBOT, which launched MMI products in 1984, was forced to delist the contract in August 1993 after AMEX refused to renew CBOT's license for the MMI.

The CME listed MMIs amid hopes the contract would trade actively next to the S&P 500 futures pit and within the CME's equity complex. As of May 1997, year-to-date volume totaled 509 contracts, with 29 contracts traded in May 1997.
"The biggest oberservation in terms of viability is the MMI," one portfolio manager said. "It just hasn't been able to go."

Several sources said logistics could also hamper arbitrage between DJIA futures at the CBOT and the CME's S&P 500 futures as the trader or dealer would have to go through two different exchanges and two separate clearinghouses.
There is also the question of budgets as futures commission merchants, looking to cut costs, must now staff two equity derivatives desks within blocks of each other.
"You've got trained equity sales people on the floor of the Merc and now you have to duplicate over at the Board of Trade," Lewald said. ((Derivatives desk 312-408-8750))
